one_line: OpenAI's inference team explains how its inference load balancer moved from a feedback-loop weight controller to a control-plane/data-plane design that optimizes end-to-end latency, plus retry budgets, outlier penalties and load shedding for production stability.
summary: Lao and Zhang, from OpenAI's inference team, describe the inference load balancer (IRB) that sits between CPU front-end clusters and GPU engine clusters and picks which engine serves each request. The original design used weighted consistent hashing, with weights set by a periodic proportional feedback loop that compared each engine's smoothed performance to the fleet average. The speakers say this was hard to reason about and caused oscillation that disrupted KV-cache locality. The new design has a control plane that computes globally optimized routing weights from live engine signals, network latency, capacity and TTFT/TBOT profiles, and publishes them asynchronously. Data-plane selectors route each request locally from the latest installed snapshot, so the request path never waits on the control plane. Nearest-engine routing is insufficient because regional demand and GPU capacity are unevenly distributed, so the optimizer minimizes expected network plus engine-side latency under hard constraints. The talk closes with protection mechanisms: outlier penalties that lower an engine's weight, utilization-dependent retry budgets to prevent retry storms, and proactive load shedding for graceful degradation. The talk is short and conceptual, with only a toy numeric example rather than production benchmarks.

key_ideas.idea: The inference load balancer sits between CPU front-end clusters and GPU engine clusters and chooses an engine per request. Routing must weigh health, capacity, locality and latency together, not only round-robin or nearest-region.
key_ideas.detail: Filter out engines that cannot serve the request (capabilities, geo or residency limits), then pick among the rest. Signals include TTFT, time between tokens, health, utilization and KV-cache locality. Follow-up turns sent to the same engine reuse cache.

key_ideas.idea: The first design used a proportional feedback loop. Weights came from smoothed engine performance compared to the fleet average, and the speakers say it was close to a PID controller.
key_ideas.detail: Weights were fed into weighted consistent hashing. The trade-offs were that it was hard to explain why one engine got a given weight, that tuning one aspect disturbed others, and that uneven GPU types made it harder.

key_ideas.idea: The feedback loop oscillated. Shifting traffic off an engine cooled it, the controller read that as spare capacity, and traffic bounced between engines, which hurt KV-cache utilization.
key_ideas.detail: This was the stated motivation for rethinking the architecture.

key_ideas.idea: Routing is split into a control plane with a global view and data-plane selectors that decide locally. Only the request path is synchronous, and it is local.
key_ideas.detail: The control plane combines live engine signals with offline regressions of capacity, TTFT and TBOT, and publishes routing weights per CPU cluster. Data planes refresh candidate engines and weights in the background, and they collect fast local signals such as ready replicas and engine health.

key_ideas.idea: Nearest-engine routing fails when demand and capacity are geographically unbalanced, so routing should minimize end-to-end latency rather than keep traffic local.
key_ideas.detail: Speaker example: one cluster sends 90 RPS to a 100 RPS nearby engine, which is fine. Another sends 120 RPS to a 100 RPS nearby engine, so 20 RPS would queue. A third region uses 40 of 80 RPS, so it has spare room. Sending the overflow to a farther engine can reduce total latency.

key_ideas.idea: The optimizer objective is expected end-to-end latency, which includes network distance and engine-side queueing. It runs under hard constraints: all traffic is routed, effective capacity is respected, and weights are non-negative.
key_ideas.detail: Its inputs are per-cluster request rates, network latency to each engine, available capacity and health, and TTFT/TBOT latency profiles as load rises. Its output is per-cluster routing fractions.

key_ideas.idea: Production protection has three layers: outlier penalties, budgeted retries and load shedding. Each is meant to stop a local failure from becoming a system-wide one.
key_ideas.detail: Outliers get reduced weight rather than being removed, so transient problems can recover, or a human can rotate out faulty hardware. Retries are capped by a budget that is dynamic, allowing more retries when the system is healthy than when it is heavily utilized. Under sustained overload, traffic is shed proactively so the system degrades gracefully instead of tipping over.

techniques.name: Control-plane / data-plane routing split
techniques.how: A control plane aggregates live engine signals and offline capacity and latency profiles, computes routing weights, and publishes snapshots. Each data-plane selector keeps the latest snapshot locally, refreshes it asynchronously, and picks an engine per request with no call to the control plane.
techniques.when: Many front-end clusters need globally consistent routing decisions, but per-request coordination would add latency to the request path.

techniques.name: Latency-minimizing routing weights
techniques.how: Solve for per-source routing fractions that minimize expected network latency plus engine-side latency, using TTFT/TBOT latency curves as load rises. Enforce that all traffic is routed, capacity is not exceeded, and weights are non-negative.
techniques.when: Demand and GPU capacity are not balanced by geography, so the nearest engine can be overloaded while a farther one has spare room.

techniques.name: Outlier penalty by weight reduction
techniques.how: When an engine behaves as an outlier, reduce its routing weight instead of removing it outright. It can recover on its own, or an operator can rotate it out.
techniques.when: Engines fail in ways that are often transient, and hard ejection could cause its own capacity loss or flapping.

techniques.name: Utilization-dependent retry budget
techniques.how: Cap retries as a budget that tightens as utilization rises, so retries cannot multiply load on a saturated system.
techniques.when: Retries are standard, but near overload they produce a retry storm that drives more failures and more retries.

techniques.name: Proactive load shedding
techniques.how: When capacity cannot meet demand, shed a fixed portion of traffic in advance so the remaining requests get acceptable service.
techniques.when: Demand exceeds what production capacity can serve, and tipping over would hurt all users.

numbers.claim: Toy example: a 100 RPS nearby engine receiving 90 RPS in region 1 is fine. Cluster B sends 120 RPS to a 100 RPS engine, so 20 RPS would wait. Region 3's 80 RPS engine uses only 40 RPS, leaving 40 RPS spare. These are illustrative numbers, not measured production results.
The talk gives no production benchmark, latency, cost or adoption figures. The only quantitative content is the illustrative RPS example.

hot_takes: Feedback loops that auto-balance on many combined signals are hard to reason about and can oscillate, which damages KV-cache locality.
Round-robin breaks cache locality, and keeping every request on the nearest region is wrong when capacity is geographically unbalanced.
Retries can make an overloaded system worse, so the retry budget should shrink as utilization rises.

relevance.why: L1 Govrix Scout does strategy routing and budgets, and L2B InferCraft runs multi-engine serving on one GPU. The talk's retry-budget, outlier-penalty and snapshot-routing ideas map directly onto both.
relevance.action: In the Govrix Scout strategy router, make the retry budget a function of current engine utilization, and penalize outlier engines by reducing their weight instead of ejecting them.
